extracted.intended_audience: USCIS/DHS policymakers, immigration adjudicators, immigration attorneys, advocates, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and application guidance for the public charge inadmissibility ground (INA 212(a)(4)), including which applicant categories are subject or exempt, available waivers/bonds, and a proposed regulatory definition of “public charge.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of INA 212(a)(4) and filing Form I-944
rubrics_metrics.description: For each immigrant / adjustment category, indicates whether the applicant is subject to INA 212(a)(4) and must file Form I-944, Declaration of Self-Sufficiency (e.g., certain Special Immigrant categories, refugees/asylees, diplomats, diversity immigrants, victims, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented in tables (Table 7–9) showing category-by-category determinations (Yes/No), with statutory citations (e.g., INA 101(a)(27)(I), INA 209(c), Section 13 of Pub. L. 85-316). Footnotes explain exceptions (e.g., some applicants are subject to INA 212(a)(4) but affidavits of support are inapplicable because employers are not relatives or for-profit entities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of INA 213A and Form I-864 (Affidavit of Support)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each category, indicates whether INA 213A and the Form I-864 Affidavit of Support are required or the category is exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables list which classes are 'Required or Exempt' with statutory and regulatory citations (e.g., INA 245(h), 8 CFR 245.12, Pub. L. citations). Notes explain statutory exemptions by category (e.g., certain refugees, diplomatic classes, diversity visas) and special cases where an affidavit is inapplicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond availability and cancellation (Form I-945 / I-356)
rubrics_metrics.description: If found inadmissible based on the public charge ground, USCIS may permit the alien to post a public charge bond (Form I-945); a public charge bond may be cancelled (Form I-356) under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bond cancellation may occur upon the alien's death, naturalization (or otherwise obtaining U.S. citizenship), or permanent departure, if the alien did not receive any public benefits as defined in the proposed rule. This is discretionary on USCIS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from the public charge inadmissibility ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has specifically exempted certain groups from the public charge inadmissibility ground (they are not subject to INA 212(a)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated exemptions include: refugees and asylees at admission and adjustment (sections 207(c)(3) and 209(c)); Amerasian immigrants at admission; Afghan and Iraqi interpreters/employees of or on behalf of U.S. Government (various NDAA and Afghan Allies Protection Act provisions); Cuban and Haitian entrants; Cuban Adjustment Act applicants; NACARA beneficiaries; HRIFA beneficiaries; Lautenberg parolees; Special immigrant juveniles (section 245(h)); applicants under section 249; Temporary Protected Status applicants (INA section 244(c)(2)(ii) and 8 CFR 244.3(a)); various diplomatic and certain nonimmigrant classes (specified statutory/regulatory citations). The text gives statutory citations and notes program sunset dates where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver eligibility for public charge inadmissibility (proposed 8 CFR 212.23(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists categories of applicants Congress has authorized to apply for waivers of the public charge inadmissibility ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes nonimmigrants admitted under section 101(a)(15)(T) (trafficking victims) at time of adjustment under 245(l)(2)(A); S nonimmigrants (alien witness/informant) under 101(a)(15)(S); applicants under 245(j) (alien witness/informant); and 'other waivers ... permissible under the law.' The proposed regulation reference (8 CFR 212.23(b)) frames waiver availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed regulatory definition of 'public charge'
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to define a public charge as an alien who receives one or more public benefits, as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states this definition aligns with legislative history, case law, and 'ordinary meaning' and notes consistency with PRWORA objectives. The proposal ties 'public charge' to receipt of public benefits (financial support from public funding) rather than other non-public forms of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard: 'likely at any time to become a public charge' (focus on future likelihood and self-sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory ground renders an alien inadmissible if he or she 'is likely at any time to become a public charge' (INA 212(a)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS emphasizes Congressional objectives in PRWORA that aliens 'should not depend on public resources ... but rather rely on their own capabilities and the resources of their families, their sponsors, and private organizations.' The proposed rule frames determinations around future likelihood and sustained self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of past receipt of public benefits in public charge determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Past receipt of welfare or public benefits alone does not automatically establish that an alien is likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Matter of Perez) indicates adjudicators should consider whether the alien can remedy past reliance on public support; inability to show capacity to overcome dependence (Matter of Harutunian, Matter of Vindman) has led to inadmissibility. DHS highlights that remedial capacity is 'a critical role' in determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core evaluative focus: whether burden of support will be on the public (not on relatives or private sponsors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge analysis emphasizes whether the alien will be 'supported at public expense' — i.e., a money charge upon the public rather than on relatives or private sponsors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court interpretations (Ex parte Kichmiriantz, Ex parte Mitchell, In re Keshishian, Coykendall v. Skrmetta, Iorio v. Day) emphasize dependency on public support as the defining feature. DHS proposes to equate 'public charge' with receipt of public benefits (public funding) rather than support from relatives or sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition nuance: 'public charge' does not necessarily require primary dependence on government
rubrics_metrics.description: Although older definitions referenced 'care, custody, management, or support of the public' or 'primary dependence,' DHS does not believe that primary dependence is required for a public charge finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes that receipt of financial support from public funding (i.e., public benefits) is sufficient for considering someone a public charge, citing dictionary definitions (Merriam-Webster, Black's Law) and rejecting a strict primary-dependence threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of vulnerable populations and distinct public policy goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain applicant classes are recognized as vulnerable (persecuted, victimized, or with little private support) and their admission serves distinct public policy goals separate from the general immigration system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule notes that many exempted classes are vulnerable and require government protection/support; this context informs exemptions and waiver policy. DHS also notes other legal provisions may permit waivers under section 212(a)(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of support inapplicability when employer is not relative or a for-profit entity
rubrics_metrics.description: For some categories (noted in footnotes), although applicants are subject to public charge under INA 212(a)(4), the requirement for an affidavit of support under INA 213A (section 212(a)(4)(D)) is inapplicable because the employer would generally not be a relative or a for-profit entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnotes in the tables explain these specific exceptions for categories such as certain international organization employees, U.S. Armed Forces personnel, and international broadcasters; statutory citations accompany the explanations.
